title: Heart
source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 19.1 Heart Anatomy; 19.5 Development of the Heart

main.t: The four-chambered muscular pump in the middle of the chest that drives blood round the lungs and the body.

simpler.t: The heart is a pump about the size of your fist. It pushes blood all round your body.

deeper.t: The right side of the heart feeds the pulmonary circuit; the left side feeds the systemic circuit.

facts.t: It lies in the mediastinum, between the lungs, inside the pericardial sac.
Its base, where the great vessels attach, is at the level of the third costal cartilage.
Its apex lies just left of the sternum, between the fourth and fifth ribs near their cartilages.

simpler.t: It sits behind your breastbone, pointing down and to the left.

deeper.t: Its right side is turned forwards and its left side backwards. The left lung has a notch for it.

items.name: Atria
items.t: The two upper chambers. They receive blood and push it into the ventricles.

items.name: Ventricles
items.t: The two lower chambers, the main pumps: right to the lungs, left to the body.

items.name: Valves
items.t: Tricuspid and mitral between atria and ventricles; pulmonary and aortic at the exits.

items.name: Septa
items.t: Walls between the chambers: interatrial, interventricular and atrioventricular.

items.name: Myocardium
items.t: The thick middle layer of the wall, made of cardiac muscle that pumps the blood.

simpler.t: Four chambers, four one-way valves and a thick muscle wall.

deeper.t: Its muscle cells swirl round the chambers in figure-of-eight patterns, which helps it pump efficiently.

facts.t: The left ventricle’s wall is much thicker than the right’s, to pump against the higher resistance of the systemic circuit.
Papillary muscles tighten the chordae tendineae as the ventricles contract, so the valve flaps cannot blow back.
The semilunar valves are pockets that fill with blood flowing back, sealing the exits.

simpler.t: Thick walls for pumping hard, and valves that let blood go only one way.

items.name: Pericardium
items.t: A tough fibrous sac with a serous lining that protects the heart and holds it in place.

items.name: Aorta
items.t: Leaves the left ventricle through the aortic valve, carrying blood to the body.

items.name: Pulmonary trunk
items.t: Leaves the right ventricle and divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries.

items.name: Coronary arteries
items.t: The first branches of the aorta. They supply the heart muscle itself.

items.name: Pulmonary veins
items.t: Bring oxygen-rich blood from the lungs into the left atrium.

simpler.t: Big vessels leave from its top, and its own arteries wrap round its surface.

facts.t: It is the first organ to work, beating from about day 21 or 22 after fertilisation.
It forms from mesoderm as a tube, which folds into an S shape between days 23 and 28.
In the fetus, the foramen ovale lets blood pass from the right atrium to the left. It closes at birth.
As many as 20–25 percent of people have a patent foramen ovale, mostly without symptoms.
An endurance athlete’s heart can be much larger than average, as exercise adds myofilaments.

items.injury: A coronary artery blocked by atherosclerotic plaque.
items.damaged: The heart muscle the artery supplies, which dies (myocardial infarction).
items.cannotDo: Keep the heart pumping normally; there is often sudden pain beneath the sternum.
items.why: Without blood and oxygen, the cardiac muscle cells die.

items.injury: Fluid or blood building up quickly in the pericardial cavity.
items.cannotDo: Fill and empty the heart fully: less blood is pumped with each beat.
items.why: The fluid presses on the heart and stops it relaxing fully between beats.

items.q: Explain why the left ventricle’s wall is thicker than the right’s.
model: Both ventricles pump the same amount of blood per beat.
The left pumps into the long systemic circuit, with high resistance.
The right pumps into the short pulmonary circuit, with low resistance.
So the left must generate much more pressure.

items.q: Compare the atrioventricular and semilunar valves.
model: Atrioventricular valves lie between atria and ventricles: tricuspid on the right, mitral on the left.
They are held by chordae tendineae and papillary muscles.
Semilunar valves guard the pulmonary trunk and aorta.
They are pocket-like, with no chordae tendineae or papillary muscles.

items.q: Predict what happens if chordae tendineae on the mitral valve break.
model: The cusps are no longer held as the ventricle contracts.
A cusp is forced backwards into the atrium (prolapse).
Blood flows back into the left atrium (regurgitation).
A heart murmur is heard with a stethoscope.

check.stem: Which chamber pumps blood into the aorta?
check.why: The left ventricle ejects blood into the aorta through the aortic semilunar valve.

check.stem: Which valve lies between the left atrium and the left ventricle?
check.why: The mitral (bicuspid) valve guards the opening between the left atrium and ventricle.

check.stem: Which vessels carry oxygen-rich blood into the heart?
check.why: The pulmonary veins return highly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
